items: “Do you have any questions or concerns?”

content_groups.group_title: Q1. Where should the vacuum cup be placed?

blocks.text: Over the fetal scalp at the appropriate flexion point on the sagittal suture, behind the anterior fontanelle, so that traction promotes flexion of the fetal head.

content_groups.group_title: Q2. Why is the flexion point important?

blocks.text: Correct placement promotes flexion of the fetal head and facilitates delivery through the smallest appropriate presenting diameter.

content_groups.group_title: Q3. What should you check before traction?

blocks.text: Correct fetal position and station, correct cup placement, absence of maternal tissue beneath the cup, adequate suction/seal and that all prerequisites for operative vaginal delivery are fulfilled.

content_groups.group_title: Q4. In what direction should you pull?

blocks.text: Along the pelvic axis, progressively following the curve of the birth canal rather than pulling directly upward.
No. It should be controlled and coordinated with contractions and maternal pushing, with reassessment of descent after each traction effort.

content_groups.group_title: Q6. What does repeated cup detachment suggest?

blocks.text: It may indicate poor cup placement, poor seal, incorrect fetal position, deflexion, excessive traction or that operative vaginal delivery is inappropriate or failing.

content_groups.group_title: Q7. What is the most serious neonatal complication you are concerned about?

blocks.text: Subgaleal haemorrhage, because it can result in significant blood loss and neonatal hypovolaemic shock.

content_groups.group_title: Q8. How do you distinguish cephalohaematoma from subgaleal haemorrhage?

blocks.text: Cephalohaematoma is confined by the sutures, whereas subgaleal haemorrhage can cross sutures and can result in substantial blood loss and shock.

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What if there is no descent?

blocks.text: Stop and reassess rather than applying further traction. Reassess position, station, cup placement, maternal and fetal condition and the possibility of disproportion. Seek senior assistance and consider an alternative mode of delivery.

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What if the CTG deteriorates during the attempted vacuum?

blocks.text: I would immediately reassess the fetal and maternal condition, stop the procedure if appropriate, call for senior assistance and expedite delivery by the fastest safe route.

items: “What are the key principles of vacuum delivery?”

blocks.text: “I would ensure that all prerequisites for operative vaginal delivery are fulfilled, confirm the fetal position and station, place the cup correctly over the flexion point, ensure no maternal tissue is trapped, apply suction according to the device protocol and use controlled traction along the pelvic axis during contractions and maternal pushing. I would require progressive descent and would stop and reassess if there is no descent, repeated cup detachment, fetal deterioration or any concern about safety.”
VACUUM DOES NOT REPLACE THE MOTHER'S PUSH — IT ASSISTS IT.
